intro: The Git mental models and commands that come up in interviews and on the job.

entries.medium: add copies changes into the index, commit turns the index into a commit and moves HEAD. The working directory is untouched by commit, which is why partial staging works.
entries.detail: reset modes differ in which trees they touch: --soft moves HEAD only, --mixed also resets the index, --hard resets all three and discards work.

entries.short: Merge preserves history; rebase rewrites your commits onto a new base.
entries.medium: Merge adds a merge commit and keeps hashes. Rebase replays your commits with new hashes for a linear history. Rebase only unpublished, personal branches; merge to integrate.
entries.detail: Rebasing a shared branch forces everyone to recover, so the rule is: rebase to update, merge to integrate.

entries.short: reset rewrites local history; revert adds an inverse commit.
entries.medium: reset moves the branch pointer and is a rewrite, so it is for local work. revert creates a new commit that undoes an earlier one and is safe on shared branches.
entries.detail: For a published mistake, always revert. Rewriting published history breaks everyone who has pulled.

entries.short: Undo changes to files and the index.
entries.medium: git restore file discards working-directory changes; git restore --staged file unstages without touching the file. It replaces the old overloaded checkout of a path.
entries.detail: These are the safe, non-history commands to reach for when you have not committed yet.

entries.short: A record of everywhere HEAD has been.
entries.medium: Reflog lists every HEAD position with a timestamp, including commits orphaned by reset, rebase and amend. Recover with git branch rescue <sha>.
entries.detail: It is the safety net for almost every accidental history change, and it only works before garbage collection prunes the objects.

entries.short: A force-push that fails if the remote moved.
entries.medium: git push --force overwrites the remote unconditionally. --force-with-lease refuses if someone else pushed since your last fetch, so you cannot silently clobber their work.
entries.detail: Better still, protect main on the remote so force-push is rejected outright. Published branches should be treated as immutable.

entries.short: Replace the last commit, before it is pushed.
entries.medium: git commit --amend adds staged changes to the previous commit or lets you edit its message. It rewrites that commit, so only use it before the commit is published.
entries.detail: Forgetting to add a file to the last commit is the classic use case.

entries.short: Copy one commit onto the current branch.
entries.medium: git cherry-pick <sha> applies a single commit elsewhere, which is useful for backporting a fix to a release branch without merging the whole feature.
entries.detail: It creates a new commit with a new hash, so the same change can end up twice in history. Use it deliberately.

entries.medium: git stash saves working-directory and index changes and cleans the tree, so you can switch branches. git stash pop reapplies them. Untracked files need -u.
entries.detail: Stashes are easy to forget and can conflict later, so prefer a small WIP commit on a branch for anything you will come back to.

entries.short: One main branch and very short-lived feature branches.
entries.medium: Branches live hours to a day and merge often, with feature flags hiding unfinished work. This keeps merges small and pairs with continuous integration and delivery.
entries.detail: Git Flow, with develop, release and hotfix branches, suits versioned releases but produces large merges. Choose by release cadence.

entries.short: Git cannot reconcile two edits to the same lines.
entries.medium: Resolve by editing the markers, then git add the file and continue the merge or rebase. git merge --abort or git rebase --abort backs out.
entries.detail: Conflicts are smaller and rarer when branches are short. A rebase can surface the same conflict once per replayed commit, which is a reason to keep branches current.

entries.short: Binary-search history to find the commit that broke something.
entries.medium: git bisect start, mark a good and a bad commit, and Git checks out the midpoint. Test, mark good or bad, and repeat until it names the culprit.
entries.detail: git bisect run automates it by running a script that exits zero for good and non-zero for bad, which turns a manual hunt into one command.
